name: Italian Game
summary: Start with 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. Build an active center, castle, and learn how your plan changes against the Giuoco Piano, Two Knights and Hungarian defenses.

chunks.title: Introduction: Develop With a Purpose
chunks.summary: Develop two kingside pieces while contesting the center. The bishop eyes f7, but king safety and central support come before an attack.
keyIdeas: Nf3 develops with an attack on e5; Bc4 develops toward f7 and helps control d5.
Black's third move tells you what to address: ...Bc5 develops actively, ...Nf6 attacks e4, and ...Be7 prepares a compact defense.
A bishop aimed at f7 is a source of pressure, not permission to sacrifice without calculation.

plans.white: Castle and choose d3 for a supported center or prepare c3 and d4. Adapt to Black's third move.
plans.black: Develop, castle and look for a supported ...d5 break to challenge e4 and free the pieces.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Develop toward f7 and clear f1 for castling. The bishop also controls d5; attacking f7 does not mean a sacrifice is already sound.

comparison.explanation: 3.Bb5 is the Ruy López: it attacks e5's defender on c6. Bc4 instead points directly toward f7 and controls d5. Both are good openings.

checkpoint.prompt: Where can the f1 bishop develop while helping control d5?
checkpoint.answer: Bc4 develops the bishop, eyes f7 and clears f1 for castling. The plan is coordinated development before an attack.

questions.prompt: Choose the central pawn move that starts this 1.e4 repertoire.
questions.hint: Open the diagonal for the f1 bishop.
questions.explanation: 1.e4 claims central space and frees the f1 bishop. 1.d4 is also a strong opening, but leads to a different repertoire.

questions.prompt: Black has played ...e5. Develop while attacking that pawn.
questions.explanation: 2.Nf3 develops with a threat to e5 and clears g1 for castling. Nc3 is sound, but does not attack e5.

questions.prompt: Develop the bishop to the Italian square, with an eye on f7.
questions.hint: Use the diagonal from f1 toward c4.
questions.explanation: 3.Bc4 starts the Italian and controls d5 while looking at f7. 3.Bb5 is the equally sound Ruy López; this course chooses Bc4.

chunks.title: Giuoco Piano: Prepare the Center
chunks.summary: Against 3...Bc5, use a quiet d3 and c3 setup. Prepare d4 instead of assuming you must attack f7 immediately.
keyIdeas: d3 supports e4 and opens the c1 bishop; it is a useful developing pawn move.
c3 supports a future d4 and gives Bc4 a retreat on c2, but temporarily takes c3 away from Nb1.
Both sides can play for a central break. White should watch ...d5 while preparing d4.

plans.white: Develop Nb1, often via d2, and the c1 bishop. Prepare d4 with enough support; do not rush it merely because c3 has been played.
plans.black: Develop the c8 bishop and seek ...d5 when supported. Consider bishop retreats if White gains central space.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Develop toward f7 and clear f1 for castling. The bishop also controls d5; attacking f7 does not mean a sacrifice is already sound.
Black mirrors the active bishop development. Both sides now have pressure toward the opposing king's starting square.
Supports e4 and opens the c1 bishop. White chooses a slower buildup instead of immediately opening the center.

comparison.explanation: 4.c3 is an ambitious alternative preparing d4 immediately. Our d3 setup supports e4 first and gives the learner a slower game; c3 is not an error.

line.note: Develops and attacks e4, which is now defended by d3.
Secures the king before spending more time on pawn preparation.
Supports e5 and opens the c8 bishop. Black chooses a solid central foundation.
Supports d4 and provides the bishop a route back through b3 to c2. The b1 knight will need another route while c3 is occupied.

comparison.explanation: 6.Nc3 develops more quickly but blocks the c-pawn's route to c3. Choose c3 here because the intended pawn break is d4; neither setup wins by force.

checkpoint.prompt: You want to play d4 later. Which pawn can help support that break?
checkpoint.answer: c3 prepares d4. Notice the cost too: Nb1 cannot develop to c3 while your pawn occupies that square.

line.note: Black secures the king, preparing to contest the center safely.
Adds a rook defender to e4. This can help White prepare d4 without leaving e4 loose.

questions.prompt: Black developed the bishop to c5. Support e4 and open your c1 bishop for a quiet setup.
questions.explanation: 4.d3 supports e4 and opens the c1 bishop. The sharper 4.c3 is also sound, but requires readiness for ...Nf6 and tactical play after d4.

questions.prompt: Your e4 pawn is supported and the kingside is clear. Secure the king.
questions.hint: Use the king and rook together.
questions.explanation: 5.O-O makes central play safer. Pawn preparation can follow after the king leaves the center.

questions.prompt: Prepare a later d4 while leaving your e-pawn in place.
questions.hint: Use the c-pawn to support d4.
questions.explanation: 6.c3 reinforces d4 and gives the bishop a future retreat, but blocks Nc3. The plan needs further development; c3 alone does not make d4 immediately best.

chunks.title: Two Knights: Answer the Central Threat
chunks.summary: After 3...Nf6, protect e4 with d3 and finish development. Understand the sharper Ng5 option without needing its forcing variations.
keyIdeas: ...Nf6 attacks e4 immediately. A move that develops can also create a threat you must address.
d3 defends e4 and opens the c1 bishop; Ng5 is a different, sharper system, not a forced response.
After ...Be7, Black aims to castle and free the center with ...d5. Support your own center before expanding.

plans.white: Develop Nb1 and Bc1, then assess d4. If Black plays ...d5, calculate the central exchanges rather than continuing your setup automatically.
plans.black: Use ...d5 when sufficiently supported to challenge e4 and activate the bishops. Avoid drifting into a passive position.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Develop toward f7 and clear f1 for castling. The bishop also controls d5; attacking f7 does not mean a sacrifice is already sound.
Develops with an attack on e4. Unlike ...Bc5, this move asks White a direct question about the center.
Defends e4 with a pawn and opens the c1 bishop. White chooses a supported buildup over the sharp Ng5 attack.

comparison.explanation: 4.Ng5 directly attacks f7 and is a legitimate sharp choice. Black can reply ...d5 5.exd5 Na5, gaining activity against Bc4. d3 chooses a quieter struggle rather than claiming an immediate win.

checkpoint.prompt: What did Black's last move threaten, and how can White address it while helping another piece?
checkpoint.answer: ...Nf6 attacks e4. d3 supports that pawn and opens the c1 bishop's diagonal.

line.note: Develops the bishop quietly and prepares castling. Black keeps c5 free and may later challenge the center.
Secures the king while e4 is already supported.
Black also castles; central pawn breaks now become safer for both players.
Reinforces e4 with a rook and keeps a future d4 break in mind.
Supports e5 and releases the c8 bishop. Black will need piece activity as well as this solid pawn chain.
Prepares d4 and leaves d2 available for Nb1. White should complete development and watch ...d5.

questions.prompt: Black's knight attacks e4. Defend it with a pawn and open the c1 bishop.
questions.explanation: 4.d3 answers the threat and opens a bishop. 4.Ng5 is also sound but leads to sharp play such as ...d5 5.exd5 Na5, with very different priorities.

questions.prompt: Your center is supported. Complete king safety.
questions.hint: The f1 and g1 squares are clear.
questions.explanation: 5.O-O secures the king before further central operations. An attack on f7 is not required just because Bc4 points there.

questions.prompt: Add a rook defender to e4 before preparing c3 and d4.
questions.hint: Use the rook that castling brought to f1.
questions.explanation: 6.Re1 reinforces e4 and prepares central play. It is a useful repertoire move, not a forced response; c3 is a sound alternative move order.

chunks.title: Hungarian Defense: Take Central Space
chunks.summary: Black's 3...Be7 is compact. Use d4 to claim space, then develop rather than trying to punish a sound defense with a forced attack.
keyIdeas: ...Be7 prepares castling and keeps the bishop away from an immediate d4 tempo.
d4 is attractive because Black has not yet played ...Nf6 to attack e4.
After ...exd4 Nxd4, the knight belongs in the center. Develop the remaining pieces and watch Black's ...d5 break.

plans.white: Develop Bc1 and connect the rooks. Use central activity rather than a speculative attack against a castled king.
plans.black: Develop the c8 bishop, coordinate the rooks and prepare ...d5 to challenge White's space.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Develop toward f7 and clear f1 for castling. The bishop also controls d5; attacking f7 does not mean a sacrifice is already sound.
Develops the bishop to a safe square and prepares castling. Black accepts less immediate activity than with ...Bc5.
Claims more central space and attacks e5. Black has not yet increased pressure on e4 with ...Nf6.

checkpoint.prompt: Black has developed the bishop but has not attacked e4 with ...Nf6. How can White use the time?
checkpoint.answer: Play d4 to claim central space. Follow central exchanges with development and castling rather than assuming Black's quiet defense is a blunder.

line.note: Exchanges the e5 pawn for White's d-pawn, relieving the tension and opening lines.
Recaptures with a developed knight in the center. The queen stays at home; 5.Qxd4? would lose her to the c6 knight's ...Nxd4.

comparison.explanation: 5.Qxd4? overlooks the c6 knight, which can play ...Nxd4 and win the queen. Nxd4 uses a minor piece to restore material instead. Check every opponent capture before choosing a recapture.

line.note: Develops and attacks e4. Black needs active pieces to compensate for White's space.
Defends e4 and develops the b1 knight. Now both knights influence the center.
Releases the c8 bishop and keeps a compact position. Black can later aim for ...d5.
Secures the king before more pieces join the center.
Black finishes king safety. White's greater space is useful, but the game still requires a plan.

questions.prompt: Black chose the quiet ...Be7. Claim the center with your other central pawn.
questions.explanation: 4.d4 takes space before Black adds pressure on e4 with ...Nf6. A quieter d3 setup also works; d4 makes immediate use of the available center.

questions.prompt: Black exchanged on d4. Recapture while keeping your queen at home.
questions.explanation: 5.Nxd4 restores material and centralizes a knight. The tempting 5.Qxd4? loses the queen to ...Nxd4 from c6. Recapturing with the most valuable piece is not automatically safe.

questions.prompt: Black attacks e4 with ...Nf6. Defend it by developing your remaining knight.
questions.hint: The b1 knight can reach c3.
questions.explanation: 6.Nc3 defends e4 and develops. It is useful because White has already played d4, so the c-pawn does not need c3 to prepare that advance.
